detail.abstract:
Background: Influenza incidence trends are jointly influenced by multiple factors, making accurate forecasting challenging. Existing forecasting methods have difficulty simultaneously capturing multiscale disease dynamics, the complex effects of external environmental variables such as meteorological conditions, and dynamic interregional transmission relationships. We aimed to develop a unified spatiotemporal forecasting framework that addresses these limitations.

Methods: We propose VMDP-Net (Variable-fused Multi-scale Dynamic Propagation Network), a spatiotemporal forecasting framework that integrates multiscale temporal features, meteorological factors, and interregional transmission relationships to jointly model short-term fluctuations, medium-term variations, and long-term trends in influenza activity. The framework comprises four modules: a Multi-scale Temporal Encoding (MTE) module that decomposes historical influenza sequences; a Multiple Variable Fusion (MVF) module that incorporates meteorological variables and enables adaptive selection of information relevant to the current epidemic stage; a Regional State Construction (RSC) module that builds unified regional node representations; and a Dynamic Mix-hop Propagation (DMP) module that adaptively learns dynamic interregional relations and captures both direct and indirect transmission effects. The model was evaluated on nine years of global influenza data, 23 years of influenza data from the United States, and nine years of influenza data from China.

Findings: VMDP-Net achieved good forecasting accuracy and stability across different spatial regions, variable configurations, and forecasting horizons on all three datasets. The framework effectively captured the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of influenza transmission and the dynamic relationships among regions. In univariate forecasting, VMDP-Net achieved the lowest mean RMSE across the five horizons on all three datasets. In multivariate forecasting, the corresponding five-horizon mean RMSE was 7.8% lower on GlobalFlu and 4.5% lower on ChinaFlu.

Interpretation: By jointly modelling multiscale temporal dynamics, meteorological drivers, and dynamic interregional transmission within a unified framework, VMDP-Net provides methodological support for real-time, coordinated public health early-warning systems.

title: The Systematic Tracking Error: Two Measurement Biases in the Estimation of Replication Risk

detail.title: The Systematic Tracking Error: Two Measurement Biases in the Estimation of Replication Risk

detail.abstract: Tracking error is routinely related to benchmark volatility, and the relation is found to be strong. We show that two standard construction choices make much of it arithmetic. The first is aggregation: averaging the tracking errors of N funds diversifies nothing and delivers a quantity 1.74 times the tracking error of the aggregated portfolio, which is what the diversification argument implies. The second is the estimation window: when tracking error and volatility are both standard deviations computed on overlapping windows, they co-move by construction. On 377 weeks of European fund data the estimated elasticity falls from 0.421 to 0.184 to 0.027 as the overlap is removed, and volatility measured inside the estimation window explains 92 per cent of the variation while volatility from the preceding non-overlapping window adds nothing. We propose normalised replication risk, tracking error per unit of market volatility; the unit exponent it imposes is not rejected, the elasticity estimated in levels being 1.04 with an interval of 0.77 to 1.31. We illustrate the correction on the entry into force of MiFID, where the uncorrected series produces a mean shift at the regulatory date with a t-statistic of 6.05 while the corrected one places the break in December 2008 and distinguishes no candidate date from a randomly chosen one, at any normalising exponent between zero and 1.6.

detail.abstract: Medical image analysis plays a crucial role in disease diagnosis and clinical decision-making; however, manual evaluation is time-consuming and requires considerable expertise. Unlike segmentation-based approaches, this study focused on the binary classification of fundus images into Cataract and Normal categories without applying image segmentation. A transfer learning approach based on the VGG19 convolutional neural network with ImageNet pre-trained weights was developed to improve classification performance by utilizing representative visual features learned from a large-scale image dataset. The proposed model was trained and evaluated to establish an accurate and reliable framework for automated cataract classification. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, sensitivity, specificity, and learning curves to evaluate classification capability and generalization performance. The results demonstrated that the pre-trained VGG19 architecture effectively extracted discriminative features and achieved reliable binary classification performance, confirming the suitability of transfer learning for ophthalmic image analysis. Automated cataract detection using deep learning may reduce the workload of ophthalmologists, improve screening efficiency, and facilitate early diagnosis. Although the findings indicate that artificial intelligence can support medical image analysis and clinical decision-making, these systems should serve as decision-support tools rather than replacements for physicians. Ethical, legal, and clinical responsibilities require that final diagnostic decisions remain under the supervision of qualified healthcare professionals. Overall, transfer learning with VGG19 represents an effective and practical approach for automated cataract classification from fundus images.

title: The Tracking Error You Are Quoted Is Too High: Asynchronous Valuation in Passive Fund Returns

detail.abstract: Weekly return differentials of passive equity funds against their own benchmarks are strongly negatively autocorrelated. Across twenty-eight European trackers the median first-order coefficient is minus 0.315, bootstrap intervals exclude zero for twenty-two of them, and it reaches minus 0.529 among exchange-traded funds against minus 0.152 among traditional index funds. This is the signature of asynchronous valuation between a fund and the index it tracks, and it has two consequences. Aggregating the differentials to two weeks and re-annualising lowers tracking error by 26 per cent for the panel and 47 per cent for exchangetraded funds, each significant at better than one per cent, so the weekly figure contains a reversal component of at least that size; the two-week figure is itself an upper bound on the true level. Under covariance stationarity the two are linked by an exact identity, the ratio being the square root of one plus the first-order coefficient, which turns the diagnostic into a calibration applicable to any quoted number. Second, conditional statistics estimated weekly can be spurious. Treynor-Mazuy and Henriksson-Merton regressions applied to these funds produce what looks like large negative market timing, with a downside beta of 1.16 against 1.04 on the upside and an apparent shortfall of 8.2 per cent a year in falling markets; it reverses within one week and flips sign under aggregation. Since passive funds do no timing, the result is a diagnostic rather than a finding, and we set out how to avoid it.

title: Market or Manager? Decomposing Replication Risk with the Systematic Tracking Error
affiliations: NEOMA Business School

detail.abstract: When a fund misses its benchmark, part of the miss belongs to the manager and part to the market. We separate them with the systematic tracking error, the standard deviation of the return differential of the aggregated portfolio, which is what survives when replication risk is pooled across funds. On twenty-eight European equity funds observed weekly from 2003 to 2013 we report three findings. Replication risk converges quickly in the number of funds: drawing subsets at random, the systematic tracking error falls from 13.65 per cent for a single fund to 8.79 for the full panel and reaches within five per cent of that floor at nine funds. The manager share of replication risk is cyclical rather than trending: splitting forty independent thirteen-week blocks at the median level of the VSTOXX, the ratio of the average fund tracking error to the systematic one is 1.752 in the calm half and 1.608 in the turbulent half, so the manager share falls from 42.9 to 37.8 per cent when markets are disturbed. A counterfactual decomposition attributes about half of that fall to the rise in correlation between funds and most of the remainder to the dispersion of their volatilities. The exercise is conducted on non-overlapping blocks throughout, so none of it rests on the overlapping-window correlation that contaminates rolling estimates.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents an interdisciplinary and conceptual framework that models the behavior of the integrated psychopath through advanced microeconomics, contract theory, and Game Theory. In the initial relational phase, the analysis captures how the amoral sender exploits an asymmetric information scenario using false cooperation signals to capture high-value assets. In response, we introduce the variable of an active receiver with a high Intellectual Quotient (IQ) who, through a continuous Bayesian filtering process, detects camouflage anomalies and executes an Optimal Stopping Rule before the discard, applying an inelastic rationing of information. Finally, the Longitudinal Bifurcation by Age Hypothesis is postulated, demonstrating how the drop in vital energy at age 50 acts as a biological exogenous shock that breaks the camouflage mask; the high-ability profile performs an invisible social withdrawal toward high-return markets or submissive micro-environments, while the conventional profile collapses endogenously into exposed verbal hostility and low-energy cynicism, converging symmetrically at age 80 due to neurobiological decline and an irreversible monopoly of intellectual isolation.

In the second phase, the model expands into organizational hierarchies under an incomplete contracts framework, formalizing the strategic transition from adverse selection during recruitment to active moral hazard post-capture. It demonstrates how the agent halts all investment in relational capital and executes asset cannibalization to extract short-term corporate rents. This exploitation drains organizational efficiency and forces a contraction in parallel agents' response functions, shifting the firm from its productivity frontier toward an Inefficient Nash Equilibrium characterized by institutional paralysis and internal market failure.

title: Machine Learning And The Donor–Recipient Dual-Risk Problem In Heart And Lung Transplantation: A Systematic Review And Meta-Analysis
affiliations: University of Pavia, Cardiovascular Department, Intermountain Medical Centre, Emory University, University of Pennsylvania and Lund University

detail.title: Machine Learning And The Donor–Recipient Dual-Risk Problem In Heart And Lung Transplantation: A Systematic Review And Meta-Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Seven of the 78 included studies were authored by review authors: EMH co-authored Hsich; EGP co-authored Peyster and Kim, and JN co-authored Medved, Lisboa, and Linse; Only Medved and Lisboa contributed to a pooled estimate; the leave-one-out analysis reported in the Results covers their removal. Author-linked studies were handled only by reviewers who were not authors of the study concerned (Contributors). We otherwise declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence could support decision-making in heart and lung transplantation, but the performance of these models and how much we can trust the evidence remain unclear. We assessed their applications, performance, and certainty of the evidence through a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods: We searched six databases and two trial registries for studies published between Jan 1, 2018, and June 30, 2026, using non-linear machine learning as the primary analytical method for survival, waitlist mortality, post-transplant complications, quality of life, or health-economic outcomes in adult thoracic transplantation. Extraction followed CHARMS and TRIPOD+AI. We assessed risk of bias and evidence certainty using an adapted PROBAST-based rubric and an adapted GRADE framework. We pooled AUROC within organ–outcome groups with at least three studies using random-effects meta-analysis. Post hoc analyses compared machine-learning and linear models within the same cohorts. PROSPERO: CRD420251174511.

Findings: Of 3340 records, 78 studies were eligible. Sixteen (21%) reported external validation; 72 (92%) had unclear or high risk of bias in the analysis domain. For 1-year survival after heart transplantation (ten studies), pooled AUROC was 0·690 (95% CI 0·649–0·729; 95% prediction interval 0·562–0·794; I²=95%). Eight studies shared a registry; retaining one estimate per data source widened the confidence interval to 0·464–0·858. For 1-year survival after lung transplantation (six studies), pooled AUROC was 0·758 (95% CI 0·568–0·882; I²=98%). In 13 same-cohort comparisons of 1-year survival, machine-learning models had higher AUROC in 11 (median difference +0·040; p=0·0002). Certainty was very low for all pooled outcomes.

Interpretation: Machine learning showed a small advantage over linear models for 1-year survival, with smaller gains in the three externally validated comparisons compared with the internally validated ones. Clinical value remains uncertain because calibration and net benefit were inconsistently reported. Richer data may improve prediction, but this needs to be tested.

detail.abstract: Crypto-asset markets increasingly depend on technological systems that determine not merely who can participate, but who can observe, process, interpret and act on market information most effectively. This paper develops the concept of Invisible Market Power (IMP): a form of market power that may arise from the cumulative interaction of data access, liquidity intelligence, computational capacity, latency, connectivity, automation and execution infrastructure, even where conventional indicators such as market share or ownership concentration do not reveal dominance. The framework identifies four core channels-latency and connectivity advantage, computational and data superiority, liquidity intelligence, and information-to-execution inequalityand extends them to institutional execution outside a retail-visible order book, latent liquidity associated with hidden or reserve orders, premium information access, and data-processing asymmetries. It further examines how market participants may infer-not directly observe-possible stop-loss clusters and liquidation-sensitive price regions, and how such estimates may inform the timing and execution of large parent orders. The paper introduces Institutional Invisible Liquidity (IIL), the Execution-Visibility Gap (EVG), Latent Order-Book Liquidity (LOBL), and an Invisible Market Power Index (IMPI), and proposes falsifiable hypotheses and an empirical identification strategy for Bitcoin spot and derivatives markets. The regulatory contribution is a measurement framework focused on technological capability, execution access, liquidity integrity, and non-discriminatory infrastructure rather than technological equality. The paper is conceptual and does not claim that the proposed mechanisms have already been empirically established. The paper also specifies a reproducible public-data pilot, a minimal formal model, and an identification strategy; these are research designs, not completed empirical estimates.

detail.abstract:
Background: Anticoagulation constitutes the cornerstone for acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT) treatment. Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of patients still develop post‑thrombotic syndrome (PTS) despite adequate anticoagulation. Multiple adjunctive therapeutic strategies have been proposed to improve long‑term clinical outcomes, yet the optimal option remains unclear, and comprehensive benefit‑risk comparisons across competing interventions are limited.

Methods: We performed a systematic review and network meta‑analysis (NMA) of randomised controlled trials (RCTs). PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library were searched up to 21 September 2026. Primary outcome was PTS incidence; secondary outcomes included all‑cause mortality, pulmonary embolism (PE) incidence, venous thromboembolism (VTE) recurrence, and bleeding‑related adverse events. Frequentist random‑effects NMA was implemented; Bayesian NMA served as sensitivity analysis. Stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA) was applied to conduct preference‑free benefit‑risk assessment incorporating four critical clinical outcomes.

Findings: Forty eligible RCTs involving 5432 participants across 80 treatment arms were included. Compared with standard anticoagulation, venoactive drug therapy (RR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.20‑0.69), thrombolytic therapy (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.34‑0.87), and compression stocking therapy (RR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.54‑0.98) significantly reduced PTS risk. Venoactive drug therapy achieved the highest SUCRA value for PTS prevention. Antiplatelet therapy showed a significantly lower VTE recurrence risk relative to several comparators. SMAA suggested antiplatelet therapy had the highest first‑rank acceptability (39.01%), while interventional therapy presented more stable overall ranking performance. Confidence factors were low for all strategies (≤ 0.50), indicating substantial uncertainty in benefit-risk rankings. Substantial within‑design heterogeneity was observed across studies.

Interpretation: Venoactive drug therapy, thrombolytic therapy and compression stockings therapy reduce PTS risk compared with standard anticoagulation therapy. No single intervention demonstrates consistent superiority across all efficacy and safety endpoints. Benefit‑risk trade‑offs should be considered for individualised DVT management.

detail.abstract: Mean-variance portfolio optimization measures risk through the covariance matrix of asset returns, but it does not directly penalize concentration. This paper examines two related specifications. Replacing the covariance matrix with an identity matrix yields mean-concentration optimization, in which the quadratic objective is the sum of squared portfolio weights. Adding that identity-matrix term to the original variance objective yields a three-criterion framework involving expected return, covariance risk, and concentration. At each target return, the investor minimizes portfolio variance plus η times concentration. The paper derives analytical solutions, characterizes the efficient set, and establishes that increasing η weakly reduces concentration and weakly increases variance at a common return target. A supplied in-sample illustration covering 41 international blue-chip stocks in Swiss francs shows how the additional penalty broadens portfolio allocations over substantial portions of the solution path while moving portfolios away from the conventional mean-variance frontier. The paper connects this trade-off to portfolio norm constraints and diagonal regularization.

detail.abstract: A bond curve converts a set of bond prices into discount factors, zero rates and forward rates for any maturity. When the curve must reprice every bond exactly, the bond prices determine only integrals of the instantaneous forward rate. The behaviour of the forward between bond maturities is therefore decided by modelling choices: the quantity that is interpolated, the interpolation scheme, and the calibration method. This paper examines those choices. We show how the choice of state variable (forward rate or zero rate) fixes the smoothness of each derived curve, and we review the main interpolation schemes, including the monotone convex method of Hagan and West. We explain why exact-fit curves built on point values of the forward are unstable, using a one-line recursion that produces an alternating "sawtooth". We describe a global Newton calibration with an analytic Jacobian, which also yields the curve's sensitivity to each input bond without numerical bumping. Six interpolation schemes are compared on 46 US Treasury bonds. All of them reprice every bond to within 4 × 10^-12 per 100 nominal, but the smoothness of their forward curves differs by almost three orders of magnitude, and monotone convex interpolation produces the smoothest forwards. We also treat spread curves as z-spread term structures over a benchmark. Throughout, worked examples and figures explain each result in plain terms.

detail.abstract: We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession. In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade. In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline. The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality. More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.

detail.abstract: Credit constraints and other demand distortions are pervasive in lower-income contexts. A model of clean technology adoption shows that demand distortions can increase the welfare gains from green subsidies. This arises through two channels: shifting the marginal adopter toward higher private and social benefits, and increasing demand elasticity. We test this by cross-randomizing purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies, and access to an interest-free loan for a US$84 induction stove among 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya. Usage subsidies of 75% have a precise zero effect on adoption and usage. Purchase price subsidies, however, generate large welfare gains. Credit constraints raise the subsidy's efficacy by 35%-73%, up to US$10-US$12 in observable welfare gain per subsidy dollar. This demand distortion also lowers the subsidy cost of abatement by 41%, to US$12 per tCO 2 e. This operates through the two channels identified in the theory: credit constraints raise the marginal adopter's positive externality by 19% and fuel savings by 30%, and lower the subsidy cost per marginal adoption by 29%. In a counterfactual without demand distortions, the abatement cost rises to US$137 per tCO 2 e. Contexts with large demand distortions could offer many cost-effective opportunities for climate change mitigation financing.

detail.abstract: How much can healthier choices reduce earnings inequality when mental and physical health both shape labor-market outcomes? We combine the United Kingdom Household Longitudinal Survey with a lifecycle model of employment and healthy choices-behavior and consumption-in which mental and physical health are separate margins and healthy choices are persistent. Persistence lets a moderate monetary cost of healthy consumption reproduce its income gradient. The model reproduces employment, healthy-choice, and health profiles by age and health state, and we use it to ask how much of the dispersion in cumulative earnings healthier choices could remove. Imposed on everyone, they reduce time spent outside good mental and physical health by 5.0% and the variance of log cumulative earnings between ages 25 and 55 by 13.4%. Mandates targeted at low offered earnings compress it further: under the P50 rule, the variance falls by 16.1%. How an intervention changes the resources that healthy choices require is central to its distributional effects.

detail.abstract: We study institutional cash management by constructing a novel dataset that records the specific money market funds (MMFs) held by each mutual fund in each month from 2010 to 2024. We document remarkably high inertia: more than half of mutual funds never switched their MMF choice throughout the sample period, despite non-negligible yield dispersion. To decompose the sources of this inertia, we develop a two-stage structural model that separately identifies the determinants of portfolio managers' attentiveness ("waking up") and their conditional preferences once attentive. We estimate the model using a methodology that combines BLP-style contraction mapping with maximum likelihood. We establish three main findings. First, MMFs with less attentive investor bases engage in greater liquidity transformation while offering lower yields. As a result, they earn higher profits and exhibit significantly higher survival rates, especially during periods of low interest rates. Second, we find that aggregate flows appear more yield-sensitive during low interest rate periods (the well-documented "reaching for yield" phenomenon) not because individual investors become more yield-seeking, but because a larger fraction of investors becomes attentive-a composition effect rather than a preference shift. Third, counterfactual analysis reveals a potential tension between market efficiency and financial stability if AI-driven automation reduces investor inattention. In the absence of inattention, fees fall by approximately half, yield dispersion collapses to near zero, and market concentration declines by roughly 20%, but monthly fund flows increase by about three times and the incidence of fund-months in which redemptions exceed a fund's weekly liquid assets rises by about six times, raising the risk of fire sales and MMF runs.

detail.abstract: Venture capital specializes in the financing of customer capital intensive firms-firms with higher sales and marketing expense to revenue ratios, a higher wage bill for sales and marketing employees, and a higher tendency to apply for trademarks-and they do so more than other financial intermediaries. Venture capitalists target high customer capital industries with low knowledge capital but avoid high knowledge capital industries that lack customer capital. Firms tilt investment toward customer capital leading up to the initial venture capital investment, after which their scale accelerates rapidly. Venture capitalists focus on financing customer capital because such investments require tolerance for substantial risks of failure in pursuit of extreme upside potential, as characterized by power law returns. This return profile fits customer capital investments more closely than investments in knowledge capital. Venture capitalists that sprinkle small investments across a large number of firms, colloquially referred to as the "spray and pray" strategy, target customer capital industries for investment, whereas venture capitalists that commit larger amounts to a small number of firms target knowledge capital industries. The venture capital focus on customer capital reflects a shift away from its traditional focus on knowledge capital intensive firms over the past 30 years.

detail.abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based virtual staining has transitioned from image-translation demonstrations into computational pathology workflows spanning label-free histology, stain-to-stain transformation, virtual immunohistochemistry, special-stain synthesis, and multiplexed representations. This review synthesizes 89 peer-reviewed original studies identified through a structured multi-database search and organizes the literature along four independent axes: staining task, source modality, source–target correspondence, and model family. We compare paired conditional GANs, unpaired and contrastive translation, transformer-based context modeling, and diffusion-based generation, and examine how supervision regime, correspondence quality, and acquisition physics constrain what each architecture family can learn. The synthesis shows that no model family is uniformly superior, and that reported gains from diffusion or attention-based models remain conditional on data quality, conditioning, sampling, and evaluation design. This study further relate image-level metrics to pathology-oriented, reader-based, reliability, and whole-slide deployment evidence, and propose a claim-matched evaluation framework in which architecture choice is interpreted jointly with task, source information, correspondence, uncertainty, computational scalability, and intended use.

detail.abstract: Does the expansion of agribusiness at the agricultural frontier improve welfare in the rural municipalities it reaches? This paper tests that hypothesis in Matopiba, Brazil, where soybean area grew from about 0.7 to 5.2 million hectares between 2000 and 2022. We combine annual land-use maps (MapBiomas, 1985-2025), nighttime lights (DMSP and VIIRS), building footprints (Google Open Buildings) and municipal indicators of income, employment, health, education and inequality for 1,163 Cerrado municipalities. Identification relies on staggered difference-indifferences (Callaway and Sant'Anna, 2021), sensitivity analysis to violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth, 2023), and long-difference instrumental variables based on the potential technological gain in soybean yields (FAO-GAEZ). Agricultural expansion raises formal agricultural employment by about 15% but produces no detectable welfare gains. Infant mortality, school quality (IDEB), the municipal human development index, poverty and income inequality do not respond in any specification. Municipal seats do not change either: urban area, building stock and urban nighttime lights remain stable, and the confidence interval rules out urban light gains above about 7%. The roughly 6% increase in GDP per capita cannot be distinguished from the growth path treated municipalities were already on before the expansion. The frontier transforms the countryside, but not the towns or the living conditions of the people who live there.

detail.abstract: Supply chain organizations operate amid demand volatility, labor shortages, disruption risk, and rapid technological change. These conditions make workforce planning inseparable from operational planning and continuous human resource development. This conceptual review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, natural language processing, and optimization can support workforce-demand forecasting, skills gap analysis, labor allocation, and targeted learning. Drawing on established research on AI in human resource management (HRM), responsible algorithmic systems, and AI enabled supply chain management, the paper synthesizes potential benefits alongside organizational and ethical constraints. The review argues that AI should be treated as decision support embedded in a socio-technical system rather than as an autonomous replacement for managerial judgment. A proposed framework links supply chain signals and workforce data to predictive analytics, human-reviewed staffing decisions, capability development, and iterative evaluation. It emphasizes data quality, explainability, privacy, fairness, worker participation, and the alignment of learning investments with changing operational requirements. The literature remains fragmented: AI-in-HRM studies often emphasize recruitment and employee outcomes, whereas supply-chain AI research typically prioritizes forecasting, inventory, and logistics performance. Consequently, the workforce implications of AI-driven supply chain planning require more longitudinal, multi-site, and worker centered investigation. The paper offers practical guidance for integrating AI enabled planning with reskilling, internal mobility, and responsible governance, while identifying testable propositions for future empirical research. No new experiments or primary data are reported.

detail.abstract:
Machine learning is increasingly used in consumer credit scoring to improve risk discrimination
and lending profitability. However, its growing reliance on extensive borrower information raises
regulatory concerns regarding algorithmic fairness and data minimisation. Existing methods
typically address these objectives separately and treat decision thresholds as pre-specified or
independently calibrated, despite their influence on both profitability and fairness. This study
proposes a nested multi-objective feature selection framework that jointly considers lending
profitability, fairness, and data minimisation. At the inner level, each candidate feature subset is
evaluated across a range of thresholds to identify its non-dominated profitability–fairness frontier.
At the outer level, the inner frontier is incorporated into an evolutionary search over feature
subsets to approximate the three-objective global Pareto frontier. Empirical evaluations across
three credit-scoring datasets, eight benchmark methods, and two measures of lending-decision
disparities show that the proposed framework identifies a diverse set of competitive solutions,
many of which remain non-dominated against competing methods. The resulting frontier enables
lenders to select feature subset–threshold combinations that balance profitability, fairness, and
data minimisation according to their operational preferences and regulatory considerations.

detail.abstract:
Background: Despite calls for increased investment in child maltreatment prevention and early family support, governments globally continue to spend funds disproportionately on downstream statutory intervention and out-of-home care (OOHC). The aim of this study was to investigate whether prevention and early family support expenditure patterns were associated with subsequent changes in child protection service outcomes.

Methods: Data from all Australian states and territories between 2015–16 to 2024–25 were included. Associations between expenditure and subsequent child protection service outcomes were examined using one-year lagged models. Expenditure on prevention – through family support services (FSS) – and early family support – through intensive family support services (IFSS) – was operationalised as: absolute (total cost per child); proportional (proportion of expenditure allocated to FSS and IFSS relative to total expenditure); demand-adjusted (cost per child subject to a child protection notification); and needs-adjusted (cost per developmentally vulnerable child). Child protection service outcomes included: children and families commencing IFSS; new and repeat child protection clients; new care and protection orders; and entry into OOHC.

Findings: Higher expenditure on FSS was consistently associated with lower rates of repeat child protection clients and entries into OOHC, with effects strongest when expenditure was needs-adjusted for population-level developmental vulnerability. Higher expenditure on IFSS was associated with increased rates of children and families commencing these services, and increased rates of new child protection clients.

Interpretation: Results show that child protection outcomes are sensitive to investment decisions. Investing in prevention is critical to reducing downstream demand for statutory intervention and OOHC.

detail.abstract:
Financial chirality, the part of an option surface that the put–call reflection reverses,[1] is a scale-dependent property.  Fractional derivatives supply the scale. They come in mirror pairs, a left-sided operator that reads lower strikes and a right-sided operator that reads higher strikes; the put–call reflection exchanges the two, and the pair decomposes exactly into an achiral Riesz part and a chiral Hilbert part rotated by ∓απ/2.  At the price level, the right-sided derivative of order α of the chirality function at the money forward is a Mellin moment of that function and defines a fractional handedness ηα.  Its member of order −2 is the global handedness η, and as α → 1, after rescaling by 1 − α, it converges to the at-the-money forward slope of the chirality function, which is exactly proportional to the smile slope: global and local chirality are endpoints of one continuous family.  At the density level, the analogous index is a signed fractional absolute moment of the half-tilted distribution.  Both families vanish under put–call symmetry and, under stated regularity conditions, vanishing over an open interval of orders is equivalent to it.

On daily S&P 500 surfaces from 2010 to 2015 at five maturities, every order is left-handed, the window moves from the wings to the forward as the order rises, and the coupling between global and local chirality differs systematically from an independent-wings benchmark and changes with maturity.  Fractional order is also an observability parameter: at the median, quoted strikes recover 99.8% of the half-order handedness at one month but only 47.8% of η.


[1]Detailed notation is given in Annexure A.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in human resource management (HRM), supporting activities such as recruitment, workforce planning, learning, performance management, and employee analytics. These applications may improve workforce productivity by reducing administrative friction, improving the allocation of skills, and helping managers identify development needs. They may also support retention through more timely career development, workload planning, and analysis of turnover risks. However, the same systems can intensify surveillance, reproduce historical inequalities, obscure decision logic, and weaken employee autonomy when deployed primarily as instruments of control. This conceptual review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature on AI-enabled HRM and workplace outcomes, with particular attention to the mechanisms connecting AI adoption to productivity and employee retention. Rather than treating AI as an inherently beneficial intervention, the paper argues that outcomes depend on system design, organizational purpose, data quality, employee perceptions, and the extent of meaningful human oversight. The paper identifies gaps in longitudinal evidence, cross-cultural research, and studies linking AI-enabled HR practices to objective productivity and retention measures. It proposes an integrative framework in which AI capability and HR strategy influence outcomes through decision quality, skill development, workload, trust, and perceived fairness, while leadership, organizational culture, job characteristics, and worker voice shape these relationships. Practical recommendations emphasize transparent governance, bias monitoring, privacy protection, employee participation, and evaluation against both organizational and employee-centred indicators. The framework offers a basis for future empirical testing; it does not claim new experimental findings.

detail.abstract:
The unprecedented expansion of passive investing—predominantly exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and market-cap weighted index trackers—has fundamentally restructured contemporary equity markets, now accounting for over 50% of aggregate domestic public equity assets. We emphasize from the outset that this investigation does not constitute a normative critique of passive investing; low-cost index funds have delivered undeniable welfare enhancements to retail investors by eliminating excessive management fees, democratizing capital market participation, and avoiding idiosyncratic active manager underperformance. Rather, our inquiry addresses a fundamental fallacy of composition and an acute macro-microstructural externality: while passive allocation is individually rational for single market participants, its aggregate dominance starves the continuous double auction of price-sensitive, information-gathering capital.

This paper formulates an ultra-high-performance, discrete-event agent-based model (ABM) implemented in Rust equipped with an endogenous Limit Order Book (LOB) executing continuous double auctions under strict Price-Time (FIFO) priority to investigate the empirical breakdown of price discovery, emergent liquidity black holes, and systemic crisis vulnerabilities as passive market share (α) escalates. Incorporating heterogeneous market participants—fundamental value mean-reversion traders facing stochastic jump-diffusion information, Avellaneda-Stoikov inventory-optimizing market makers, adaptive Brock-Hommes switching traders, noise and momentum trend-followers, and systematic TWAP indexers—we execute extensive, embarrassingly parallel Monte Carlo simulations sweeping α ∈ [0.0, 0.95] across K = 100 independent seeds and T = 200,000 discrete ticks per regime (totaling 240M ticks across 1,200 trajectories). We calibrate event arrivals and Pareto order size distributions (α_size = 1.7436, implied CCDF tail μ_tail = 0.7436) against empirical Level 3 LOBSTER data from NASDAQ (N = 100,000 events, T_obs = 1,998.57 s).

Our results demonstrate that market efficiency does not degrade linearly; rather, markets experience an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory with an acute phase transition around a critical threshold α* ≈ 0.85. Beyond α*, fundamental order flow is insufficient to anchor prices, resulting in a sharp surge in tracking divergence (RMSE(P, V) escalates from 1.6670 at α = 0.60 and 1.7113 at α = 0.50 to 1.9605 at α = 0.85, 2.0185 at α = 0.90, and 2.8599 at α = 0.95, an expansion of +71.6%), order book depth starvation (D_bid → 0), and severe leptokurtic fat tails (κ rising from 3.56 at α = 0.70 and 4.09 at α = 0.80 to 5.42 at α = 0.85 and 12.37 at α = 0.95). Furthermore, high-precision semi-parametric Geweke-Porter-Hudak (σ(d) = 0.0224, bandwidth m = 823) and Robinson Local Whittle estimates confirm stationary fractional volatility dynamics across all regimes (d ∈ [0.1368, 0.3899]). In addition, an endogenous Brock-Hommes evolutionary simulation demonstrates that rational information cost economization drives α_t from initial low levels directly into this critical fragility zone (α* ≈ 0.85). Finally, adversarial stress testing demonstrates the microstructural mechanisms of predatory front-running and short raids, while macroeconomic crisis shocks encounter liquidity vacuums where panic redemptions trigger price overshoot ratios reaching 4.27× at α = 0.85 and 7.04× at α = 0.95. These findings provide formal microstructural evidence for the Grossman-Stiglitz informational paradox under passive market saturation and offer actionable market design recommendations to preserve the virtues of indexation while safeguarding financial stability.

detail.abstract: Overly broad market definitions can misrepresent local resource access, leading to inefficient place-based policy targeting. We develop a new framework to measure consumer-level access by modeling utilization flows flexibly across overlapping spatial markets. Applying it to U.S. Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) designations, we estimate that 11.6 million people lack adequate access to primary care physicians (PCPs), far fewer than the 30 to 80 million identified by HPSAs. Simulations indicate that increasing PCP supply by under 1.4% could eliminate shortages nationwide. Our findings underscore the importance of a flexible measurement framework and offer actionable guidance for improving primary care access.

detail.abstract: Organizations use relationship-oriented HR practices such as collective rituals to cultivate cohesion. Such practices are often associated with shared positive affect, collective engagement, and lower turnover rates. Yet little is known about how these practices may impact retention outcomes under dynamic staffing conditions. Drawing on cohesion, turnover, and socialization literatures, we develop the concept of brittle cohesion to explain why relationship-oriented practices and the cohesion-related states they foster can buffer hiring disruptions but amplify vulnerability under exit disruptions. Using 14 months of administrative and survey data from 1,620 retail stores, we find that collective ritual engagement is positively associated with shared positive affect and collective engagement, which are negatively associated with unit-level voluntary turnover. During hiring surges, higher ritual engagement and stronger cohesion-related states are associated with weaker increases in voluntary turnover among both newcomers and incumbents. However, voluntary turnover surges are associated with declines in cohesion-related states, which are associated with subsequent turnover, particularly in highly ritual-engaged units. Together, these findings illustrate brittle cohesion: relationship-oriented HR practices and the cohesion they foster can strengthen retention during hiring disruptions, while their retention benefits become fragile during exit disruptions, revealing an important vulnerability associated with cohesion-based retention practices.

detail.abstract: AI is already widely used in strategic foresight, but there is little shared evidence on where it adds value across the process from foresight to action. This report presents a reference model for using AI in foresight, innovation and strategy, built on the 3P model of corporate foresight: Perceiving, Prospecting and Probing. This report draws on the lessons and insights from over six months of practice-based research. Working as a Community of Practice with foresight, innovation and strategy professionals from eight organisations (BMW Group, Bosch, EDHEC Business School, Equinor, Lufthansa Innovation Hub, Siemens, Thales and TÜV NORD Group) piloted and assessed AI across 25 methods of the reference model. AI proved a powerful force multiplier, but its capabilities are jagged. The gains therefore come not from maximising delegation but from designing the human–AI workflow. Three lessons stand out. First, data quality is decisive, and selecting and governing your own data will matter more, not less. Second, control your AI before it controls you: set a clear intention and plan the method, data and prompt before you start, so that checking becomes targeted rather than exhaustive. Third, hybrid intelligence is a journey, not a state. In analytical methods, AI increasingly leads while humans steer and check; in creative, value-defining methods, the roles reverse. For each method, the reference model rates whether AI use is recommended. The report also presents high-value use cases, together with workflow designs and a reusable prompt library. It also recommends five calls to action for organisations today. With frontier models evolving rapidly, the lasting advantage is less likely to come from the model an organisation uses than from its data readiness and the discipline of its practice. The road to exceptionality is making AI follow your intention; the road to catastrophe requires only cognitive laziness.

detail.abstract: This paper explores how sovereign credit spreads vary with the level of governance. An analysis of 74 countries over the 2001-2016 period shows that sovereign credit default swap (CDS) spreads decrease with government effectiveness, particularly in countries exhibiting severe default risk, high indebtedness, and poor economic conditions. We formulate a theoretical explanation for these findings using a structural model in which governments adjust default and debt policies based on their abilities to collect and use fiscal revenues. The theory posits that more effective governments have less incentive to default and thus benefit from narrower credit spreads, although they may choose higher indebtedness levels.

detail.abstract: Brazil's rapid demographic transition presents growing challenges for the sustainability, coverage, and adequacy of its pension system. Although the 2019 pension reform improved fiscal sustainability, population ageing and persistent labour informality continue to place pressure on pension financing and old-age income security. Drawing on existing research and policy evidence, this policy brief examines the trade-offs between fiscal consolidation, contributory coverage, and non-contributory income protection. It argues that future pension reform should move beyond a predominantly fiscal perspective towards an integrated social protection strategy. Three policy priorities are proposed: expanding pension coverage among informal and self-employed workers through simplified contribution mechanisms and targeted incentives; promoting active ageing and longer labour market participation through age-inclusive employment policies; and strengthening minimum income protection for vulnerable older adults. The brief concludes that financial sustainability and social protection should be pursued as complementary objectives rather than competing policy priorities.

detail.abstract: Unusual outputs from generative artificial intelligence can acquire recognizable identities and circulate as persistent cultural figures. This article proposes the pathomorphology of latent space, a comparative analytic framework examining how anomalous visual generations, persona-related language-model shifts, and digital occult practices emerge and stabilize. While retaining "latent space" as an umbrella concept, our protocol strictly distinguishes between multimodal embeddings, diffusion states, autoregressive activation streams, and parameter weights across three levels of analysis: observable model behavior and candidate mechanisms, human interpretive framing, and sociotechnical circulation. Applying an eight-point protocol, we compare three cases: the visual cryptid Loab (2022), mechanistic interpretability studies of alignment and emergent misalignment in large language models, and contemporary cyber-occult experiments (Infinite Backrooms and Truth Terminal) viewed against 1990s precursors (TIAMAT and CCRU). Conrad Waddington’s epigenetic landscape and Carl Gustav Jung’s concepts of the Shadow, Persona, and enantiodromia serve as bounded heuristic models assessed against competing technical explanations without implying a shared mathematical or psychological ontology. Ultimately, we argue that digital myth-making arises from recursive feedback among conditional model outputs, curatorial selection, and cultural recirculation, and formulate falsifiable research questions to test these dynamics. Our central distinction separates generative persistence (recurrence of specified output features under defined conditions), perceptual continuity (observers’ recognition of different outputs as the same figure), and cultural persistence (continued circulation of a named identity), where evidence for one does not independently establish the others.

detail.abstract: We compare daily CoinGecko prices for 49 DeFi tokens with Binance exchange prices from September 2025 to August 2026. Outside an 11-week window (10 January to 27 March 2026) the two sources agree to a median gap of 0.09%, and 0.10% of token-days differ by more than 10%. Inside the window 33% of token-days differ by more than 10%, and 25 of the 49 tokens are affected, including THORChain, Ondo and Jupiter; the vendor price is usually too high, by a median factor of 4.4 for API3. Market capitalizations inherit the errors: the sector’s market capitalization is overstated by a median 7.6% (up to 12.7%), a cap-weighted index of the 49 tokens is off by more than one percentage point on 40 of 77 days and shows an artificial drop of about 9 points when the errors stop, and the top-20 ranking is wrong on 69 of 77 days. A second download in October 2026 shows that the vendor has silently corrected 23% of the erroneous token-days and left 76% unchanged, so the same request returns different histories on different dates. The errors manufacture backtest performance: a factor portfolio’s Sharpe ratio is 1.78 on vendor prices and 0.76 on exchange prices, and a short-term reversal rule’s is 3.5 against 0.3. Strict return-based screens find a fifth of the affected tokens. Finally, in a pre-registered test on 21 tokens not used before, a logistic model of Santiment on-chain and social metrics does not predict which tokens beat the median over the next week (out-of-sample AUC 0.49, p = 0.67).

detail.abstract: Transparency law is built to disclose and contest decisions one node at a time. This study asks whether that stage-indexed design can detect disadvantage that arises when several individually defensible filters operate in sequence, each taking the outputs of its predecessors as inputs. The analysis combines doctrinal and functional-comparative study of the EU Digital Services Act and the Court of Justice's SCHUFA judgment, Brazil's Access to Information Law and the Supreme Federal Court's 2025 ruling on Article 19 of the Marco Civil da Internet, and U.S. procedural due process and employment-selection guidelines, with a structured reading of empirical literature on content moderation, peer review, research funding and ranking systems. It develops a model of sequential filtering with four properties: multiplicative composition, carry-forward dependence, participation exit, and path opacity. A stylised arithmetic and simulation exercise, offered as illustration and not as evidence about any institution, shows that stage-level selection-rate ratios can each remain above the four-fifths benchmark while the cumulative ratio falls below it, that audits of later stages understate the gap those stages inherit, and that carry-forward dependence amplifies but cannot originate disparity. The central thesis is that current law suffers a mismatch of unit: accountability attaches to stages, while the injury attaches to paths. The study identifies the closest existing concepts (cumulative advantage, bottom-line adverse-impact analysis, intersectionality), states what the model adds, answers the strongest objections, and derives a modest interpretive and governance consequence: path-level review wherever institutions chain filters whose outputs feed one another. Limits of inference are stated throughout.

detail.abstract: Worst-case risk evaluation is central to finance and operations research, yet existing analytical results remain fragmented and largely confined to ambiguity sets with specific structures. Using spectral risk measures as the underlying class, we develop a convex variational theory that unifies these analyses and extends them to richer ambiguity models. The theory rests on a representation principle: use the quantile or distribution formulation that preserves convexity of the full ambiguity set. In both representations, the resulting optimality conditions provide a systematic route to identify the worst-case law and determine its risk value. This approach recovers classical central-moment bounds and yields closed-form or semi-closedform solutions for practically motivated models involving Wasserstein ambiguity with tail stress, two-sided expected shortfall (ES) bands, asymmetric partial moments, geometric-moment bounds, and exponentialor Gaussian-reference Kullback-Leibler (KL) neighborhoods. Beyond these analytical results, the same theory yields projection-based algorithms with fixed-grid convergence under the stated assumptions. In a high-dimensional portfolio application, we establish an exact projection identity for mean-anchored joint KL ambiguity under a Gaussian reference. The resulting standardized worst-case ES coefficient applies to every portfolio, reducing robust portfolio selection to an exact second-order cone program after a single calibration.

detail.abstract: This paper identifies the range of well-being losses caused by climatic hazards in coastal regions of Asia and the Pacific and reviews how these losses are measured for policy and practice. It draws on a targeted review of selected studies. The review identifies nine domains of well-being loss: food security, water and sanitation, livelihoods and employment, unpaid work, mobility and displacement, health and psychosocial well-being, safety and gender-based violence, cultural and social well-being, and ecosystem loss. Existing measurement approaches are not equipped to capture these well-being losses in a comprehensive, time-effective, and cost-effective manner. A case study on Cyclone Remal in Bangladesh highlights the importance of timely, sex-disaggregated data collection using customized rapid survey tools for effective and equitable disaster response, recovery, and resilience. The paper proposes a framework for data collection and recommends key well-being indicators. It emphasizes the need to institutionalize tailored rapid survey tools within national systems and strengthen data capacity and coordination to support gender-inclusive disaster response.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses the structural question of how far Chinese enterprises can go global, and proposes the Enterprise Going-Global Boundary Model (full title: “Two-Boundary—Enterprise Six-Segment Value Chain—Cross-Border Feasible Zone—Four-Quadrant Chinese Enterprise Going-Global Boundary Model Based on National Interest and Enterprise Value Chain Roots”). While existing internationalization theories center on enterprise capabilities, this paper argues that capability alone does not determine the ceiling of an enterprise’s global reach under today’s dual institutionalization of national interests. Instead, the going-global ceiling is jointly determined by two necessary conditions: the National Interest Boundary (external necessary condition) and the Enterprise Value Chain Root Boundary (internal necessary condition). Enterprise capability, cross-border paths, and governance structures are sufficient conditions that operate only within the cross-border feasible zone permitted by both boundaries. Within the unified framework of “Two Boundaries—Enterprise Six-Segment Value Chain—Cross-Border Feasible Zone—Four-Quadrant Classification Model,” this paper identifies four structural positions for enterprises: Deep Going-Global (Quadrant I, SHEIN), Target-Country Veto (Quadrant II, TikTok), Modular Going-Global (Quadrant III, Temu/Haidilao), and High Lock-In (Quadrant IV, SMIC). Cross-national stress tests across 10 foreign enterprises and two counterexamples (Huawei and DJI) validate the model’s cross-industry applicability, discriminatory power, and robustness against counterexamples. The dual institutional validation provided by the Provisions of the State Council on Outbound Investment (effective July 2026) and the Manus case (April 2026) confirms the paper’s core proposition: regulatory look-through review asks not “where is the company registered” but “where are the enterprise value chain roots embedded,” conferring institutional foresight upon the theoretical framework. Furthermore, this paper proposes the ‘Quadrant Portfolio’ hypothesis, shifting the analytical granularity from enterprise-level to business-level, revealing the structural characteristics of multi-business enterprises where different business segments belong to different quadrants due to variations in national interest sensitivity and enterprise value chain root depth, as well as the structural tension of ‘Shared Core-Differentiated Applications’ and the paradox of ‘Technology Sharing-Compliance Separation’. This paper revises three bodies of literature: it reframes internationalization theory from capability-centrism to a two-tier boundary-capability structure; it introduces enterprise value chain structure as the missing analytical dimension in national interest research; and it transforms institutional boundaries from exogenous variables to structural determinants of value chain cross-border capacity in GVC research. For enterprises, the correct starting point of a going-global strategy is boundary assessment rather than capability evaluation. For policymakers, the transition from industrial policy to enterprise value chain policy is imperative. detail.abstract: We revisit the proposition that right-wing governments tend to promote free markets while left-wing governments constrain them, providing the first causal estimates of the effect of government leaders' ideology on economic freedom. Using a doubly-robust stacked difference-indifferences approach that accounts for staggered treatment timing, we identify clean ideological transitions following a stable pre-treatment period in a sample of 153 countries between 2000 and 2023 using Economic Freedom of the World (EFW) as the main outcome, and for a sample of 21 OECD countries extending as far back as 1870 using the Historical Index of Economic Liberty (HIEL). For the Global-EFW sample, we find no significant effects following transitions to either a left or a right-wing government. For the OECD sample, we find no evidence that a transition to a right-wing government affects economic freedom. Our two most robust findings are a negative, but small, effect on economic freedom following a transition to a left government among OECD countries, driven by a larger size of government, and a small, positive, and significant impact on economic freedom following a transition to the right among non-OECD countries.

detail.abstract: Brazilian real estate investment funds (FIIs) grew from about 121,000 investors in December 2017 to 3.2 million in May 2026, most of them individuals. Using a documentary multiple-case design, this paper examines three practices permitted by current rules that weaken the information effectively available to these investors. ALZR11 recognizes inflation adjustment on its IPCA-linked debt as an accounting expense but adds the unpaid portion back when computing distributable cash-basis income; the add-back equaled 6.2% and 5.6% of declared distributions in the fiscal years ended June 2024 and June 2025. The reorganization that wound up IRDM11 and transferred its portfolio to IRIM11, a much smaller fund managed by the same firm, moved assets at net asset value, thereby resetting the cost basis used to compute distributable gains and losses. TRXF11 financed acquisitions at capitalization rates near 8% through successive offerings settled largely with new units delivered to asset sellers, while distributing approximately 11.5% per year on net asset value. Across all three cases, the relevant facts were disclosed and, in part, audited, yet they remained outside the dividend-yield metric on which retail investors tend to rely. The paper interprets this pattern through agency theory, the incomplete revelation hypothesis, and the literature on limited attention, and proposes three low-cost disclosure improvements.

detail.abstract: Academic closure is the proportion of academics in an institution or network who are either educated within that institution or network, or who have been `carried up' through the network via connections with other insiders. In this paper, I ask whether closure can arise when academics act rationally and pursue their own private interests, without collusive agreements or explicit corruption or discrimination. I ask whether such a system can still be Pareto inefficient. To achieve this goal, I construct a simple model of nomination based admissions in which incumbents benefit privately from nominating their own connections. I assume that the benefit of screening the unconnected outsiders is shared across the whole club. Since the cost of screening is privatized by the nomination committee and the benefit is socialised, the unconnected outsiders are not screened in equilibrium even when screening them would be to the benefit of every incumbent. The model implies that membership will grow less than in proportion to the size of the pool of potential candidates and will be determined by historical incumbency. I take these predictions and apply them to a full census of the IZA@LISER network (2,336 members in 54 countries) which has been merged with World Bank data. The negative binomial models yield an elasticity of membership with respect to the national research workforce of 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.85), clearly rejecting proportional access. The large research systems of East Asia and Russia are found to have a very small share of the membership relative to their size and income, while entire regions are not represented at all. The empirical results demonstrate two hypotheses derived from the theoretical model. Namely, that conditional on the quality of national research systems, the elasticity of membership with respect to the national research workforce should be below one (H1), and second, that countries where the network's incumbency originated should be over-represented relative to their research capacity, implying that research systems without historical incumbency should be under-represented (H2).

detail.abstract: Portfolio Sharpe ratios from statistical factor models can reflect allocation choices even when return forecasts coincide. Adding a ridge adjustment to factor covariances penalizes factor exposures in units set by normalization. We derive the transformation that preserves portfolio positions across equivalent model representations. Two separately estimated IPCA normalizations deliver nearly identical forecasts but gross Sharpe ratios of 0.69 and 1.07 under the same numerical penalty; transforming the penalty consistently aligns their portfolios. Using the full fitted mean, including characteristic-associated intercepts, produces a portfolio with a gross Sharpe ratio of 2.51 and little sensitivity to the penalty.

detail.abstract: Pretrial defendants, particularly from underserved communities, face significant financial hurdles that result in inefficient capital allocation and human capital depreciation. detail.abstract: A recommender faces consumers who can verify recommendations, but differ in their attention costs or in the salience of their choice of adoption. We characterize the conditions under which a technology that increases transparency by lowering the cost of verifying a product's quality will increase or decrease false recommendations. Without commitment, reducing verification costs never increases false recommendations, but when the recommender can commit to a policy, transparency can worsen both the quality of recommendations and consumer welfare. The necessary and sufficient condition is that the log-elasticity of the distribution of consumer cost types is decreasing. It can hold when the distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, or when it mixes sophisticated and naive consumers. Our results can be applied to platformrecommended listings, security ratings, and audits.

detail.abstract: Public debate continues regarding single payor healthcare (SPH) proposals, such as Medicare for All.  Regardless of SPH's advantages or disadvantages for healthcare, one major impediment receives little recognition. When government action directly takes or financially eviscerates private property, the Constitution's Fifth Amendment deems this a Taking, for which just compensation must be paid. In the U.S., an enormous swath of healthcare insurance is investor owned. In a single payor system these plans would largely disappear, essentially overnight. Depending on how SPH were to be accomplished, long-standing Takings jurisprudence suggests that stock- and bond-holders must be compensated, at fair market value, with payment required virtually immediately. This consequence would render SPH financially unsustainable.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the design of risk-stratified benchmarking affects incentives and organizational responses under quality-based yardstick competition. Using data from 1,935 hospitals across 35 states, we study the 2018 reform to the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP) that replaced a uniform national benchmark with peer-group benchmarks defined by hospitals’ shares of Medicare-Medicaid dual-eligible patients. First, we find that hospitals experiencing larger benchmark shifts following the reform exhibit larger reductions in readmissions, indicating stronger behavioral responses when performance targets are tailored to more comparable peers. Second, we show that dual-eligible share does not consistently capture underlying socioeconomic disadvantage across Medicaid expansion and non-expansion states. Hospitals in expansion states exhibit significantly lower poverty levels and lower baseline readmission rates than non-expansion-state hospitals in the same peer group. Third, using a difference-in-differences framework, we find that these measurement differences translate into asymmetric incentive effects. Hospitals in expansion states improve less after the reform than those in non-expansion states. Finally, we propose a data-driven risk stratification framework that utilizes policy-invariant measures of socioeconomic disadvantage. Our counterfactual analysis shows that this approach produces more comparable peer groups, avoids an additional 2,344 readmissions and approximately $36.3 million in readmission costs relative to the current regime. More broadly, our results show that the effectiveness of risk-stratified benchmarking depends on whether the stratification measure accurately captures the underlying sources of systematic performance differences across organizations. In particular, we show that unrelated policies can inadvertently affect those measures, leading to unintended differences in incentives across organizations.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a conditional normative law-and-economics model of environmental policy under environmental-rights and property-rights commitments. Stronger environmental commitments raise the value government assigns to environmental quality, while stronger property-rights protection raises the cost of regulation. Given specified objectives, costs, and feasibility limits, government chooses among regulation, compensated acquisition, and inaction. Stronger property-rights protection makes regulation less attractive, but environmental effects depend on the alternative: a shift to inaction reduces quality, while a shift to acquisition increases it when acquisition delivers more quality than regulation at the switching threshold. A numerical illustration maps the highest-value instrument across 10,201 combinations of environmental commitment and regulatory burden, then examines sensitivity to parameter changes. A separate comparison with the first-best benchmark under illustrative values of the common marginal social cost parameter shows that the quality gap depends on that assumption. The results offer conditional guidance about institutional trade-offs; assessing actual policymaking requires empirical evidence.

detail.abstract: Many of the hundreds of quantities and variables that characterize the dynamics, functioning, and performance of cities exhibit power law relationships-known as urban scaling. This article derives urban scaling laws from the microeconomic foundations of the standard urban model, showing that such empirical regularities emerge endogenously from the fundamental spatial mechanisms of cities. Requiring no assumptions at all beyond those of standard urban economic theory, we demonstrate that micro-founded power-law relationships arise exactly in spatial equilibrium with respect to net income, and exhibit asymptotic scaling in population and gross income. We show that existing urban scaling theories are a consistent subset of our scaling exponents which depend explicitly only on structural economic parameters.

detail.abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

detail.abstract: Cross-border capital flows can significantly influence system-wide liquidity especially in open economies with limited or no nominal exchangerate flexibility. While steady foreign exchange (FX) inflows have boosted excess reserves in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) over the recent years, examining the macro-financial impact of external shocks to net FX flows can inform a more comprehensive, risk-based, and forward-looking assessment of monetary conditions. A simple blockwise structural VAR model indicates regime-dependent monetary transmis sion since the Dirham Monetary Framework’s inception: cross-border capital flows materially shape credit dynamics mostly when system-wide liquidity drops below its historical norm. Conversely, when liquidity is abundant, the macro-financial impact is limited. However, the findings—albeit based on limited empirical data—underscore the importance of smoothing excessive liquidity fluctuations from external shocks to ensure that monetary transmission remains effective and consistent with the stabilising role of a fixed exchange rate anchor. Ef fective liquidity management of FX flow-driven changes in system-wide liquidity rather than discretionary policy rate changes (and its interaction with credit and money markets) is the primary and obvious instrument of monetary policy operations to preserve an optimal level of liquidity surplus rather than attempting to directly steer aggregate capital flows.

detail.abstract: Spatio-temporal generalised additive models (GAMs) are routine tools for mapping malaria risk, yet they are almost always fitted with penalised smooths alone, ignoring the several layers of unobserved heterogeneity that characterise entomological surveillance data. In this study we assemble a hierarchical spatiotemporal generalised additive mixed model (HST-GAMM) that treats penalised smooths and random effects within a single mixed-model formalism, and we use it not to maximise predictive accuracy but as an analytical instrument to characterise the structure of malaria risk in the city of Yaoundé. Two complementary sources of stochastic structure are distinguished: implicit random effects, the Gaussian structure induced by the roughness penalties of the smooth terms, and explicit random effects exchangeable, nested, spatially structured (BYM2) and serially correlated components. Casting all of these as one partially improper Gaussian prior lets every variance component be estimated jointly by Laplace-approximate marginal likelihood. A five-model nested ablation (M0-M4) isolates each component's contribution, in particular separating the spatial (BYM2) and temporal (RW1) structured effects, which a coarser taxonomy had previously confounded. Neither structured component improves on a plain exchangeable neighbourhood effect in function recovery or out-of-sample prediction at this sample size, and the spatial component cannot even be evaluated under spatial hold-out, a structural limitation of per-neighbourhood graphstructured smooths. We record the identifiability tension between a smooth spatial term and an areal effect (Lemma 1) and propose a restricted-spatialregression constraint (M4c, Proposition 2); a dedicated simulation shows the constraint’s standard errors match its theoretical target exactly, yet that target a model with no areal effect at all is itself miscalibrated whenever the confounder has a genuine unstructured component, so the constraint does not restore valid coverage. We state this as a precise scope condition on the constraint’s practical usefulness, not previously articulated in the restricted-spatial-regression literature. Applied to four years of bimonthly Anopheles sporozoite data across 22 neighbourhoods of Yaoundé, combined with ERA5-Land and MODIS covariates, the fitted model reveals what a conventional or parsimonious model cannot: that spatial heterogeneity is unstructured rather than smoothly graded, that there is suggestive evidence of interannual deformation of risk (sensitive to a single year in a leave-one-out check), and that only rainfall and, marginally, vegetation not temperature carry explanatory signal. A power analysis at the exact sample size of the application confirms that a smooth spatial field of epidemiologically plausible amplitude would have been detected, so the observed absence of structure is an informative null rather than a symptom of low power. Simulation-based residual diagnostics support the negative-binomial specification, including the reproduction of the 80% zero counts. We show that these findings, which require the full model to establish, imply that for the narrower task of out-of-sample prediction a neighbourhood random intercept model suffices, and we translate the fit into an effort corrected neighbourhood risk map for targeting vector control.

detail.abstract: Our short paper aims to answer a vital question: Given the European Union's current dependence on American and Chinese AI infrastructure, how is its AI sovereign capability likely to evolve in the next decade? We describe the status quo within a Production, Infrastructure, and Application (PIA) framework. Several layers of foreign dependency are revealed which the proposed European Technological Sovereignty Package aims to reduce. Achieving sovereignty by 2035, however, faces formidable challenges in funding, raw materials, semiconductor production, energy generation, data centres, cloud computing, and competitive frontier AI models. One area where it has leverage is ASML's monopoly on EUV lithography. AI sovereignty proves most attainable in reshoring opensource models where access cannot be withdrawn. Yet the current capability and funding gap undermines even this limited sovereignty. Ultimately, to achieve the best-case scenario, European Union Member States must cooperate and confront the challenges mentioned to avoid renting out their future on a critical economic input.
