detail.abstract: An emergency collection plan may perform poorly because of its visit order, its supplier combination, or both. Separating these losses helps determine how much reordering alone can improve the plan. We study collection from distributed inventories under a prescribed policy: each pickup meets remaining demand subject to available stock, and visits stop once all material requirements are satisfied. Conditional optimization considers only orders that reproduce exactly the same realized supply-point set. It separates recoverable ordering loss from activation-set loss, the gap between that set's conditional optimum and the global optimum. We examine these losses using complete exact landscapes, parameter comparisons, and individual-plan diagnostics. Across ten complete landscapes with eight or ten candidate supply points, activation-set loss dominates under set-balanced aggregation, with median instance-level shares of approximately 79\% and 72\%, respectively. Optimal reordering therefore leaves most aggregate loss unresolved in these landscapes. Some instances and plans nevertheless retain substantial ordering opportunities. Across 70 exact parameter scenarios, emphasizing configuration-switching or loading/unloading costs increases the sequence-weighted ordering-loss share, while emphasizing coordination costs reduces it. Responses to demand changes vary across instances; activation-set loss remains dominant in the tested scenarios. We interpret these responses by examining admissible orders, realized supply allocations, and cost changes under set-preserving reordering. Individual plans can also be assessed when the global optimum is unknown, as illustrated by search-output diagnostics and a case application. Exact conditional optimization determines the maximum fixed-set improvement; heuristic search identifies attainable gains without certifying that maximum. In the case application, another feasible combination achieves an objective value below the retained set's exact conditional optimum. Matching that performance requires changing the combination. These findings suggest evaluating supplier combinations by their best admissible execution and reassessing each plan when demand or priorities change. Current objective values and aggregate loss proportions alone do not establish how much an individual plan can improve.

detail.abstract: Peer-to-peer (P2P) sharing platforms, such as Hygglo and Peerby, have created new ways for consumers to access durable goods in categories ranging from photography and outdoor equipment to power tools and cars. In these settings, sales and rentals are typically managed by separate intermediaries, namely retailers and rental providers. Yet the presence of a P2P platform links these previously independent markets through supply and price linkages, turning the retailer and rental provider into indirect competitors. We call the resulting competition among ownership, traditional rental, and platform access triangular competition. In order to examine how a P2P platform's presence affects new-product sales, rental volume, and total product ownership, we develop a stylized model in which a manufacturer distributes through a retailer and a rental provider, while consumers can also access products through a P2P platform, and product owners can offer them for sharing. Our results show that the platform's presence reshapes sales and rental markets in ways that would be missed by studying either in isolation. In the sales market, sharing income enhances the value of ownership, increasing new-product sales when the sharing fraction is sufficiently low or marginal cost is sufficiently high; neglecting the rental market understates this effect. In the rental market, we identify a cross-market expansion effect: although platform access competes directly with renting and rental consumers earn no sharing income, the platform's presence can still increase rental volume. This occurs when marginal cost and the sharing fraction are sufficiently low. We also examine whether the presence of platforms reduces product ownership, as platforms frequently claim, by considering total ownership across personally owned and rental-provider-owned products. When platform access closely substitutes for renting, total ownership increases only under limited sharing and low marginal cost. As renting becomes more differentiated from platform access, weaker rental-market cannibalization changes this pattern: with limited sharing, total ownership increases across the marginal-cost range; with more extensive sharing, it increases only when marginal cost is sufficiently high. Our findings show that understanding the interactions between sales and rental markets is essential for assessing how a platform's presence affects firms' operational decisions and total ownership.

detail.abstract: Urban delivery, especially the last-mile delivery, has become an increasingly important area in the global supply chain along with the boom of e-commerce. Delivery companies and merchants can introduce some innovative solutions such as the equipment of autonomous vehicles (AVs) to decrease their operating costs, environmental impact, and social risks during the delivery process. This paper mainly develops a mathematical model to get the best allocation of Avs among city logistics centers (CLCs) as a mixed delivery method. The advantage of the presented model stems from considering the equipment cost, the delivery cost, and the CO2 emission, which is measured through social carbon cost (SCC). In addition, this paper establishes a risk model considering the impact of seasonal variations to evaluate the infection risk of delivery during pandemic periods for four potential delivery scenarios: customers going to CLCs, ordering online and picking-up at CLCs, delivering by traditional vehicles (TVs), and delivering by the mixed method with the optimal allocation of AVs. The research finds the optimal allocation for a London case, reveals the relationship between the nominal service capacity (NCpa) of CLCs and the optimal number of CLCs equipped with AVs, concludes that the more CLCs are equipped with AVs, the fewer CO2 emissions and the fewer citizens will be infected, and provides some managerial insights that may help delivery companies and merchants make appropriate decisions about the allocation of AVs.

detail.abstract: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorumcertified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

detail.abstract:
This report examines how Brazil recruits and retains highly skilled migrants and international students, with a focus on STEM talent. Brazil faces a shortage of skilled workers: half of surveyed firms report talent gaps, yet very few turn to foreign hiring. Immigration has also shifted toward lower-skilled, Mercosur-based flows following the 2009 Residence Agreement. Among migrant workers, the share holding an academic degree fell from about 57% (2010) to 28% (2018), and the share in STEM occupations from 29% to 14%. International students remain a marginal group, at roughly 0.1% of undergraduate enrolment, despite free public universities and programs such as PEC-G and the Institutional Internationalization Program.

The 2017 Immigration Law modernized the legal framework and eased naturalization. However, key provisions remain unregulated, including visas for foreigners with “strategic professional capabilities” (Articles 38 and 147) and the National Policy on Migration, Asylum and Statelessness (Article 120). Policies have emerged in an uncoordinated way, and gaps in migration data persist, including the delayed DataMigra portal. Drawing on stakeholder perspectives (CNI, OECD, IOM, ILO), the report recommends:

  • integrating a talent-attraction strategy into the national migration policy;
  • simplifying recruitment from outside Mercosur;
  • making higher education more attractive to international students and scholars;
  • improving data collection and transparency.

detail.abstract: This article investigates how the strategic involvement of automotive firms in electric-vehicle (EV) production is associated with financial performance and environmental efficiency. It examines three relationships: whether EV production is associated with operational eco-efficiency, whether the share of EVs in a firm’s portfolio is associated with short-term profitability (ROS), and whether lagged changes in Scope 3 emissions are associated with return on assets (ROA). The results show a positive and statistically significant association between firm size and operational eco-efficiency, alongside a negative and statistically significant association between EV production and eco-efficiency. The EV portfolio share is not significantly associated with ROS, whereas leverage is negatively and significantly associated with ROS. Lagged Scope 3 emissions changes are not significantly associated with ROA. Thus, the results do not support the hypothesis that a higher EV sales share is positively associated with operational eco-efficiency, measured by the Eco-Efficiency Ratio and the hypothesis that a higher EV sales share is negatively associated with short-term profitability (ROS). We couldn’t find the statistically significant support for the hypothesis that reductions in Scope 3 emissions (-1) intensity significantly predict improvements in long-term Return on Assets (ROA. The findings from the logistic regression analysis confirm that EV producers have higher debt and lower scope 1 emissions, whereas the evidence for profitability and operational eco-efficiency is less conclusive. The positive association between lagged Scope 2 emissions and EV-producer status (OR = 1.106, p = 0.003 in Model 1) should be interpreted with caution, i.e., that higher emissions promote EV production or that EV producers are less environmentally efficient. These findings represent associations rather than causal effects. Differences in firms’ Scope 3 measurement and reporting practices may limit the comparability of emissions data across firms and overtime.

detail.abstract: Community-based participatory research (CBPR) offers a collaborative approach to generating knowledge with, rather than merely about, communities affected by mental health policy. This conceptual review examines how CBPR can improve the relevance, legitimacy, equity and implementation of mental health policy development. It synthesizes foundational participatory research principles with recent reviews of CBPR in mental health and international guidance on meaningful social participation. The literature suggests that involvement of people with lived experience, families, community organizations and frontline workers can reveal barriers obscured by administrative data, identify culturally and locally appropriate priorities, and strengthen accountability between policy institutions and the populations they serve. However, participation is not inherently empowering: projects may reproduce professional hierarchies, over-represent organized groups, impose unpaid emotional labour, or collect community knowledge without demonstrable policy uptake. Recent evidence also indicates inconsistent reporting of partnership structures and variable adherence to core CBPR principles. In response, this paper proposes a community-partnered policy cycle linking priority setting, shared inquiry, deliberation, formal policy decisions, implementation, and public feedback. The framework emphasizes shared decision rights, compensation, accessible communication, ethical data governance and traceable responses to recommendations. The paper argues that CBPR should be evaluated not only by research outputs or individual mental health outcomes, but also by its influence on policy content, budgets, service accessibility and distributional equity. The proposed framework is conceptual rather than empirically validated. Future comparative and longitudinal studies should test which governance arrangements produce sustained policy influence across different health systems and marginalized populations.

detail.abstract: High asset price volatility alongside low portfolio flows reveals a fundamental trade-off between investor disagreement and price impact: When volatility is high but flows are small, investors must either largely agree with each other or be insensitive to price changes, implying large price impacts of small flows. We formalize this relationship in a price impact bound based on price volatility, flow volatility, and investor agreement. Applying our bound to U.S. equities yields large price impacts, implying that flows are central to understanding price dynamics. Our bounds align with event-study estimates while revealing novel patterns across horizons, assets, and aggregation levels.

detail.abstract: When funds with illiquid portfolios grow rapidly without rebalancing into more liquid assets, they generate self-inflated returns via their own price impact. Investors chase these returns, triggering a positive feedback loop that inflates both fund size and asset prices. We introduce a simple measure - fund illiquidity - that captures a fund’s potential for return inflation. Using daily ETF data, we estimate price impact, decompose returns, and show that investors chase both fundamental and self-inflated returns. We find that inflated funds underperform in the long run and that stock-level ownership by inflated funds predicts negative long-term returns.

detail.abstract:
The current theory (model) of performance, while having produced many improvements in performance during its hundred-year reign, has been essentially exhausted. This has left us with little more than a labyrinth of explanations for human performance.  Quoting the Committee on Techniques for the Enhancement of Human Performance of the U.S. National Research Council Commission on Behavioral and Social Sciences and Education (Druckman et al. 1997): “The committee is therefore unable to draw conclusions, based on scientific evidence, on what does or does not work to enhance organizational performance”

Given that models are constrained and shaped by the paradigm from within which they are generated, a truly new model of performance would require a new paradigm of performance. Our new model of performance (a part of our new paradigm of performance), rather than adding more explanations for why people do what they do and why they don’t do what they don’t do, provides actionable access to the source of human performance.  This actionable access to the source of performance opens up a new realm of opportunity for study and research, and for new and more effective interventions, applications, and practices for improving individual, group, and organizational performance.

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship research and practice have long treated the founding team, rather than the individual founder, as the normal unit of new venture creation, because a single person rarely commands the full range of functions a venture requires from its first months: opportunity research, product development, marketing, customer operations, finance and administration. Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) now perform workable versions of several of these functions, raising a question the literature has not yet organised: how far does agentic AI lower the minimum viable team — the smallest human configuration that can credibly start and operate a new venture? This conceptual paper develops a function-by-function framework that classifies six core venture functions as ones agentic AI can largely substitute, ones it can augment under founder direction, and ones where founder judgment must remain reserved. Building on effectuation, the resource-based view and the automation–augmentation paradox, I argue that AI relaxes the execution constraint on founding without relaxing the judgment constraint; as execution becomes abundant, founder judgment, and the trust and distribution a venture can command, become the scarce resources that differentiate ventures. I identify three risks of the shift — homogenised ventures, over-delegation and capability hollowing — draw implications for founders, accelerators, educators and policymakers in emerging economies, and derive three testable propositions for empirical research.

detail.abstract: Purpose: Oilfield service companies in the Gulf staff much of their field work through manpower suppliers. The supplier holds each contractor's visa and work permit and acts as the employer of record. When procurement teams reduce the number of these suppliers, they apply a logic built for purchased goods to a workforce of sponsored people. This paper builds a conceptual framework that shows when such consolidation protects workforce continuity and when it damages it. Design/Methodology/Approach: The paper synthesizes theory. It combines transaction cost economics, resource dependence theory, research on single versus multiple sourcing, research on triadic employment, and sustainable human resource management into one model. Findings: One mechanism separates manpower consolidation from goods consolidation: sponsorship-bound switching cost. A client cannot move a worker between suppliers without responsoring that worker, so switching cost grows with headcount and depends on where each permit sits in its cycle. Consolidation therefore lowers coordination costs at the price of correlated disruption risk, dependence on one sponsor, and pressure on contractor retention and safety behaviour. Eight propositions connect supplier concentration, transition timing, and supplier-panel design to cost, continuity, and resilience. A typology separates big-bang consolidation, rolling consolidation, static panels, and managed panels. Originality: The paper is the first to treat the sponsored worker as the relationship-specific asset in supply-base reduction and to present migration timed to permit expiry as a resilience tool. Practical Implications: Managers should time transfers to permit renewal, keep one qualified secondary supplier, and track contractor retention and safety participation alongside the rate savings. For firms certified to API Specification Q2, the secondary supplier also gives auditable evidence of contingency planning for a critical supplier.

detail.abstract: Spare-parts pooling can reduce duplicated inventory across manufacturing sites, yet an available shared component does not necessarily restore production promptly. Transport, competing requests, qualified labour and shutdown access can determine whether inventory sharing improves equipment availability. This paper asks under what conditions pooling should accompany corrective, preventive or condition-based maintenance when financial, staffing, skill and scheduling resources are constrained. A structured critical review of verified scholarly sources is combined with an original analytical comparison of restoration times. The study uses no operational dataset, simulation or estimated performance results. Its contribution is a conditional decision test that distinguishes earlier part arrival from earlier restoration, using the maximum of part, crew and access readiness rather than adding overlapping delays. For otherwise identical interventions, an exact positive-part identity identifies when a change in part arrival affects downtime. A corresponding expected-cost comparison separates inventory savings from transport, administration and production-loss consequences. The analysis shows why partial pooling, local protection for time-critical components and advance reservation for planned interventions deserve consideration alongside complete sharing. It also identifies repair capacity and correlated requests as constraints that inventory aggregation alone cannot resolve. The findings provide a transparent basis for policy screening and local validation; they do not establish universally optimal stock levels or quantified savings. Manufacturing implementation requires compatible components, traceable transactions and explicit allocation rules aligned with site-level service commitments.

detail.abstract: Digital service platforms increasingly use endorsement programs to help consumers identify high-quality providers. Motivated by this, we study whether and how a planner should disclose provider quality to maximize the welfare of quality-and delay-sensitive consumers. We consider a marketplace where multiple providers, vertically differentiated in equality, offer a single type of service to consumers who differ in valuations of quality. The planner observes provider quality and chooses whether and how much information to disclose to consumers. Consumers update their beliefs and then choose joining one of the unobservable parallel queues, one for each provider, or exiting. Consumer welfare equals surplus from service net of disutility from delay. In a two-provider model, we show that disclosing information is optimal without congestion but can reduce welfare with congestion due to trade-off between assortative matching and workload imbalance. The net impact of disclosure is nonmonotonic as consumers become more sensitive to delay. With an arbitrary number of providers where the planner also chooses disclosure granularity, the problem is combinatorial. We identify sufficient conditions for either no disclosure or a two-signal policy (i.e., single-tier badge endorsement program in practice) to be optimal. Using data from an online healthcare platform, we calibrate the model and evaluate alternative endorsement designs. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for congestion externalities for platform endorsement design, and programs with only a few badge tiers can be highly effective.

detail.abstract: Authentic gratitude and appreciation are powerful catalysts for combating widespread disengagement and enhancing well-being. Drawing on neuroscience and empirical studies, this paper demonstrates how genuine recognition activates brain reward centers, reduces stress, and creates positive feedback loops that boost productivity and retention. Analysis reveals that employees who are appreciated have significantly higher engagement and loyalty. We explore practical applications through positive psychology models and leadership strategies, arguing that systematic appreciation is a strategic imperative for organizational success, not just good etiquette.

detail.abstract: Ethnic food products, which are typically introduced by immigrant groups and rooted in a country other than one's home country, are widely consumed. Retailers often employ one of two different categorization schemes to organize these products. Functional categorization groups products based on shared use characteristics (e.g., tortillas in the bread aisle). Cultural categorization creates a distinct group for ethnic food products (e.g., tortillas in the "International" aisle) regardless of use characteristics. This paper investigates whether such categorization influences the evaluation and selection of ethnic food products by native consumers. Across six studies, we find that cultural (vs. functional) categorization increases the selection of ethnic food products, driven by two parallel processes. First, the perceived typicality of ethnic food products goes up under cultural categorization, increasing evaluation and selection under cultural categorization. Second, the perceived target consumer changes (towards a consumer of another country or cultural group) under functional categorization, decreasing their selection under functional categorization. Further, the authors find that this effect is moderated by consumer ethnocentrism. The difference between cultural and functional categorization is largest for highly ethnocentric consumers, who receive the largest boost in the selection of ethnic food products under cultural categorization.

detail.abstract: Reward-based crowdfunding is an operating channel through which early-stage ventures validate demand, pre-sell offerings, and secure resources for execution. By December 2025, Kickstarter alone had attracted over $9.4 billion in cumulative pledges. Prior research shows that, unlike in conventional investment-oriented finance, female-led campaigns often outperform male-led campaigns in this channel. Securities regulators opened equity crowdfunding to retail investors in several Canadian provinces in 2015 and in the United States in 2016 to broaden access to early-stage capital. This study examines whether legalizing equity crowdfunding, an investment-oriented channel, changes outcomes for female entrepreneurs in reward-based crowdfunding. Using synthetic difference-indifferences , the study analyzes regulatory changes in Canada (Study 1) and the United States (Study 2). Across both settings, the analyses yield negative post-legalization estimates for female-led campaign success on Kickstarter, relative to the estimated counterfactual, whereas estimates for male-led campaigns are not statistically significant. The United States estimates remain nearly unchanged with an additional post-treatment year. Equity crowdfunding filings and a similarity survey document connections between the two channels. Two experiments investigate a behavioral mechanism and explore a potential platform intervention. The first experiment shows that, compared with information about reward-based crowdfunding, information about equity crowdfunding moves participants toward an investment-oriented mindset when evaluating a reward-based project, an orientation previously shown to favor male over female entrepreneurs. The second experiment examines a brief bias-awareness message encouraging fair evaluations of entrepreneurs. With the message present, support for the female entrepreneur is nearly identical under the consumption (evaluating the project as a consumer) and investment (evaluating it as an investor) decision frames, unlike the published benchmark, and the gender gaps within each frame are smaller and not statistically significant. Together, the findings identify a cross-channel consequence of policy expanding access to capital: opening one financing channel can worsen outcomes for entrepreneurs historically served well by an adjacent channel. Policy evaluation and platform design should consider adjacent channels, particularly for female entrepreneurs.

title: Integrated care for families in poverty: Professionals’ perspectives on barriers and facilitators
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences and Erasmus University Rotterdam

detail.title: Integrated care for families in poverty: Professionals’ perspectives on barriers and facilitators
detail.abstract: IntroductionPoverty is multidimensional, affecting life domains such as income, health and housing, and affects parents and children, often in different ways. Support for families in poverty should therefore address these interrelated challenges across domains. Integrated care, defined here as coordinated support focusing on multiple domains and family members, is a theoretically promising approach to meeting these requirements. The present study aims to advance our understanding of integrated care for families in poverty by examining which barriers and facilitators professionals face in daily practice. MethodSemi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 Dutch professionals, concerning 26 families in poverty, and analyzed using a preregistered mixed inductive-deductive approach. ResultsProfessionals experienced barriers and facilitators at six interrelated levels: (1) professional (e.g., being patient); (2) parent (e.g., a proactive attitude); (3) parent-professional relationship (e.g., a strong alliance); (4) organizational (e.g., being a safe haven for families); (5) collaborative (e.g., clear collegial communication), and (6) systemic (e.g., bureaucracy). Facilitators were most prominent at the professional, parent-professional relationship, and organizational levels, whereas barriers were most often reported at the parent and systemic levels. Professionals’ competencies and a strong parent-professional alliance were prominent facilitators, whereas systemic barriers limited the time and energy available to support families. ConclusionOur findings suggest supporting families in poverty depends on factors at multiple levels, not only individual-level efforts. Alongside training professionals to connect with families and build a strong alliance, policy-level changes including simplifying bureaucratic procedures are needed to realize the full potential of integrated care for families in poverty.

detail.abstract: Background. Clinicians influence whether Internet-delivered and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled interventions reach routine care. Since late 2022, web-based large language models (LLMs) have widened clinicians’ exposure to AI.Objective. To describe differences in physicians’ attitudes toward clinical AI between 2022 and 2026, a period of widespread LLM diffusion, and to examine correlates of trust in AI clinical decisions.Methods. Repeated cross-sectional comparison of two open web surveys of physicians in Italy, conducted in 2022 before the release of ChatGPT (N=500) and in 2026 (N=500), using the same eight-item attitude scale. Each item was compared between waves using mean differences and standardized effect sizes with false-discovery-rate correction. Correlates of trust in AI clinical decisions in 2026 were examined with ordinal logistic regression.Results. After correction, five of the eight items were higher in 2026, but most differences were small. The largest were for ease of use (+0.59 points; d=0.58), utility (d=0.37) and peer encouragement (d=0.29). Perceived trustworthiness did not differ (d=0.05), and perceived safety and transparency were slightly lower (d=−0.13). The composite score was 3.46 in 2022 and 3.66 in 2026. In 2026, 80.2% of respondents had used AI tools in clinical practice, but only 4.0% had received formal training and 81.4% reported low familiarity. Trust in AI clinical decisions was low (mean 2.95 out of 5) and was most strongly associated with perceived trustworthiness (adjusted odds ratio 1.94 per standard deviation, 95% CI 1.54-2.45). Governance expectations were near-unanimous (mean 4.59).Conclusions. During the diffusion of LLMs, physicians’ attitudes toward clinical AI were modestly more favorable, while trust in AI decisions remained limited, formal training rare and governance expectations high. Clinician training and accountability structures are plausible targets for implementing AI-enabled Internet interventions.

detail.abstract: Commercial websites intend to convert as many users as possible into leads or customers. To support this effort conversion rate optimisation (CRO) is used to test page variations to find the best performing designs for a website. In banking, consumers that have completed a conversion point must have submitted an enquiry or online application. Often however, consumers drop out at some stage in the user journey and leave the website. Therefore, a search of two databases was conducted that retuned 76,703 records. An additional 36 records were found in grey literature. After an initial screening and further full-text searches 59 records were included in the scoping review. To improve CRO on financial services websites, the scoping review addressed three questions. First, what is known in the literature about CRO in banking. Second, the paper investigated the internal decision-making process within banks and how it impacts CRO. Neither professional nor academic literature has addressed this issue even though websites are under regulatory and technical constraints on what can be published. Third, the scoping review investigated what is known about online consumer decisionmaking. Here the scoping review identified several fields that have investigated website performance. However, the literature is missing a holistic model that can be used to improve the different areas of decision-making. Hence a conceptual model is developed that can be applied by digital professionals to improve online experiences and therefore increase conversions. Consumers will benefit through better online experiences that result in better quality leads and applications for financial institutions.

detail.abstract: Security and network operations centers are adopting AI-driven tooling faster than anyone has studied what that adoption does to the people on the floor. This paper reports a descriptive phenomenological study of 11 frontline SOC and NOC professionals in the United States who used SOAR, UEBA, AIenhanced EDR, or generative AI assistants in daily work between 2016 and 2026. Four findings emerged. Analysts accept AI with relief and dread at the same time, and perceived usefulness does not produce acceptance while replacement anxiety is unaddressed. Trust is reactive rather than cumulative: a single confidently wrong verdict produced lasting hyper-vigilance in every analyst who experienced one. Analysts split on whether the system is a partner or a calculator, and the split tracks how they define their own job. Prompting, not deskilling, is what changed about the work. Underneath all four sits a governance flaw: operators carry full liability for outputs they cannot inspect. I close with four changes leaders can make, mapped to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, and with what the study cannot tell us.

detail.abstract: Generative AI may help investors process public information, but widespread use of the same models can make their decisions more alike. This paper asks whether common AIrelated information remains underused in stock prices or has become sufficiently reflected that further reliance produces overreaction. We derive a sign restriction from a noisy rational expectations model: conditional on the price, the common signal predicts returns positively when underused and negatively when overweighted. We test this prediction around 98,461 U.S. earnings announcements from 2015 to 2025 using a point-in-time information index and stocks' exposure to retail orders routed through brokers that later introduced AI assistants. After ChatGPT, the signal predicts announcement returns positively across all exposure groups, with a significant association among the most exposed stocks. We find no exposure-related change after ChatGPT or broker launches. The evidence is consistent with continued underreaction, rather than AI-induced overreaction, in this empirical setting.

detail.abstract: Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Lower effective quality in middle plans weakens the alternatives available to premium users, allowing higher prices for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose: broader access can coexist with utility polarization. Second, an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus by preserving some revenue that finances service while limiting degradation. Third, cheaper compute can raise quality and reduce ad intensity, yet sufficiently large cost reductions can increase aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level because better service raises the value of the remaining advertised interactions. An extension shows how advertising-funded upgrades can bring plans to the same maximum capability and advertising exposure, eliminating the basis for different prices. These results make menu design central to evaluating LLM advertising: the consequences extend beyond users who see ads to the alternatives and prices faced by those who do not.

detail.abstract: Aim To evaluate a service-oriented multi-criteria recommender system (MCRS) integrating Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and fuzzy logic to generate department-specific, patient-centric healthcare recommendations for specialized clinics and general hospitals.,Methods A service-level framework was designed using Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFNs) to handle subjectivity in structured patient ratings across five dimensions: core clinical treatment, staff competence, cleanliness, waiting time, and sentiment. Patient feedback from two public datasets (gomask.ai, n=200; Kaggle, n=1,444) was fuzzified and evaluated using linear weighted aggregation. Comparative routing was executed across six clinical departments (Cardiology, Dermatology, Neurology, Oncology, Orthopedics, Pediatrics) under three patient-priority scenarios. Centroid defuzzification determined terminal crisp scores and institutional performance gaps.,Results Specialized clinics matched or outperformed multi-specialty hospitals in specific clinical domains despite lower overall institutional infrastructure. Department 2 (Dermatology) demonstrated the largest performance gap, with specialized clinics outperforming hospitals by up to 52.95% when waiting time and treatment were prioritized. Department 4 (Oncology) exhibited the narrowest performance variance (27.16%–28.19%), indicating service parity across institution types.,Conclusion Department-level evaluation prevents the masking of specialized clinical merit by aggregate institutional ratings. Embedding QFD within an MCRS effectively routes patients to high-performing outpatient facilities, optimizing clinical utility while mitigating financial toxicity associated with unneeded auxiliary amenities.

detail.abstract: Effective disaster preparedness at the municipal scale requires real-time environmental intelligence at a resolution that national weather infrastructure was never designed to deliver. This chapter presents field deployment case studies from two Florida municipalities, the City of Cape Canaveral and the City of Altamonte Springs, where AI-integrated hyperlocal sensor networks were installed to support urban risk modelling and emergency preparedness operations. Each pilot uses commercial Davis Instruments weather stations sited at municipally owned facilities and generating continuous atmospheric, wind and precipitation data streams that are ingested by a cloud-based urban risk modelling platform. The Cape Canaveral configuration is a four-node coastal array optimised for hurricane preparedness and storm surge risk; the Altamonte Springs configuration is a three-node inland array spanning a civic centre, an arterial corridor site and a water treatment facility, addressing convective flooding and severe weather detection. Both deployments were designed for resource-constrained municipal environments, emphasising low unit cost, scalability, zero financial burden on the partner city, and compatibility with existing emergency management workflows. The chapter details site selection methodology, partnership development, and lessons learned. It further addresses deployment challenges specific to DDIL-adjacent environments, including intermittent connectivity and limited municipal information technology capacity, and the operational requirements of sustaining a pilot without dedicated technical staff on the city side. Proprietary implementation details of the analytics platform are described at a functional level only. These deployments offer a replicable model for AI-enhanced disaster preparedness in small and mid-sized municipalities, with direct implications for urban digital twin development and community-scale early warning systems.

detail.abstract: We examine how richer query information changes the revenue economics of search advertising. We model the move from keyword search to conversational search as a refinement of the platform's information about query-level click-through rates and ask how this refinement affects expected revenue under different selling rules. We find that, under a fixed weighted second-price auction, finer information weakly improves matching but has an ambiguous effect on revenue. This is because more precise queries can thin out competition within realized auctions. When the platform can adapt the mechanism to the information it observes, finer information weakly raises expected revenue. With constant demand elasticities, the revenue-maximizing auction is a weighted second-price auction with tuned weights and reserves, an auction format major platforms use. Conversational search also raises questions regarding the optimal timing of ads in a conversation. We argue that a platform may prefer to wait before showing an ad, because later turns can reveal more about what the user wants, although the user may leave before then.

title: The Economics of Independent AI Assurance: Why Self-Certification Fails When Agents Act
affiliations: AiEnsured

detail.title: The Economics of Independent AI Assurance: Why Self-Certification Fails When Agents Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Co-founder and CTO of AiEnsured / testAIng.com, which offers AI assurance services.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. Self-funded.

detail.abstract: Enterprises increasingly deploy AI systems that do not merely produce text but take actions: they call tools, move money, change records and commit organisations to transactions. Most of the evidence buyers receive about such systems is produced by the builders themselves, often through internal benchmarks or "LLM-as-judge" scoring. This paper argues, using the economics of information, that builder self-certification of agentic AI is structurally insufficient. AI assurance is a credence good: its quality cannot be observed by the buyer before or even after purchase. Unverifiable self-reports are cheap talk, which produces pooling and an Akerlof-style adverse-selection dynamic. A simple decision-theoretic argument shows that a builder who bears only part of the cost of a missed failure, and none of the cost borne by third parties, rationally sets a more lenient detection threshold than is socially optimal. Agentic failures of terminal state, authority and ordering are partly irreversible and create externalities, which widens this gap. Implications for buyers, boards and regulators are discussed in relation to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act and Indian policy context. AI tools were used for language editing and structuring; the author is responsible for all arguments and claims.
